I can often recognize the sources for biased editorials and news reports, but it is really impossible to understand how NEWSpapers ignore important NEWS about their own communities. 

 

The most recent example of obvious omission was to be found or more precisely not to be found in the Los Angeles Times, which somehow managed to ignore last weekend's NORML conference that was held in LA. 

 

There was not a word about it in any news story, even though last Friday's editorial page carried an Op-Ed by travel writer and NORML advisory board member Rick Steves, that might have been even more controversial than marijuana reform, Europe: Curing, not punishing, addicts It ended with the note he was speaking at the NORML convention in Los Angeles. (He made the opening speech.) 

 

And it isn't as though the marijuana story is not of major importance in their city. After all, there are hundreds of medical marijuana dispensaries in greater LA, and they are still being raided by the Feds, which the Times does report. (In fairness to the Times, the much smaller LA Daily News also ignored NORML.) 

 

Moreover, the Times recently made a major discovery, on a par with finding out that there is gambling in the casino, Gang rivalry grows into race war Battle over the drug trade has led to escalating violence in Florence-Firestone. 

See 

The Theory and Practice of Chaos Analysis By Richard Cowan 

 

See 

The Theory and Practice of Chaos Analysis By Richard Cowan 

 

We are told, Race, gang rivalry and drugs have become impossibly tangled as motives in killings and assaults in the neighborhood, authorities and residents say. 

 

Even this hint is progress. Believe it or not, the Times has carried stories about gang violence without mentioning the drug trade. Of course, they would never use the term drug prohibition and notice that in the body of the story it was back to just drugs as though it was about addicts fighting over a fix. Gang violence is a major problem in LA, and anything that increases the violence between blacks and Latinos should be considered a threat to the entire community. 

 

Ah yes, then there is Mexico, that country about 140 miles south of the LA Times offices. Earlier this month the Times carried a story quoting our infallible Drug Czar about his latest victory: Cocaine supply down sharply, U.S. officials say.

The article quoted Michael A. Braun, the Drug Enforcement Administration's chief of operations as saying, "Kudos go to President Calderon and his cops and military. They are very aggressively engaged and working closely with us and other U.S. law enforcement along the southwest border and Mexico in attacking the major cartels."

Good news? Well, the Austin American-Statesman (obviously not named after our President) reported on Monday, (T)here is concern on both sides of the border about the Mexican military's human rights record and its effectiveness in fighting the drug cartels. 

 

While the military's involvement was initially meant to be temporary, the aid plan could give it a permanent role. According to published reports, 40 percent of the money in the aid package would go to the military, and the rest would go to police agencies.

 

There have been other reports that the Mexican army has already been corrupted and are involved in the cross-border trafficking. In other words, the drug war is further undermining US border security, and to make matters worse, there is evidence that the violence in Mexico is crossing the border. 

 

According to a new report prepared for the Governor of Texas,There were 1,543 drug-related killings in Mexico in 2005 and more than 2,100 in 2006, and with more than 2,100 estimated since Jan. 1 it will certainly make this year the deadliest yet," the report states. 

 

Corruption is also to be found on both sides of the border. The report notes, "On the U.S. side, however, the under-reporting of crimes ... and corruption among low- and mid-level U.S. law enforcement officials facilitate the northward spread of cartel activity." 

 

Needless to say, considering the source, it never occurs to them that prohibition is the problem, so more violence must be the solution. 

 

Meanwhile back at the LA Times, violence in its city, violence on the border, violence in Mexico, all continue to escalate, but because of the blindness of the prohibitionist paradigm they cannot see its cause. Governor Schwarzenegger again vetoed the hemp bill passed by the California legislature, to great praise from the Drug Czar, and great silence from the Times.
